# Pattern Transferability and Generalization {#sec-loop-patterns-across-stack}

![](images/ch09-cover-map.svg){fig-alt="A source record meets a changed condition, after which units are carried, updated, replaced, or retired and target claims are checked anew."}

::: {.epigraph}
> "There is no single development, in either technology or in management technique, that by itself promises even one order-of-magnitude improvement in productivity, in reliability, in simplicity."
>
> — Frederick P. Brooks Jr., *No Silver Bullet* (1987) [@Brooks1986NoSilverBullet, p. 10]
:::

Architectural design rarely begins with an empty repository; new design programs inherit codebases, simulation harnesses, learned models, and historical records from prior projects (@sec-running-the-loop). When workloads, instruction set architectures (ISAs), or semiconductor process nodes change, an AI-native design system must determine what can be reused, what must adapt, and which prior conclusions need new evidence. Reusable principles, engineering components, and empirical conclusions carry different obligations.

This chapter proposes a transfer test that first asks whether the architecture decision itself has changed. Four stages then partition the source, isolate affected dependencies, assign each unit an action, and pair it with target checks. The array study retained from @sec-running-the-loop illustrates how source artifacts can help a prospective Lighthouse study while leaving its implementation decision open. Matched target-only comparisons test the benefit of reuse in decision quality and total cost, including adaptation and requalification.

## Pattern Transferability and Scope

Reusing prior design work can save engineering time, but risks carrying forward obsolete assumptions that invalidate new decisions. Prior work divides into three kinds, each carrying a different verification burden.

1. *Core principles and methodology* transfer broadly because they govern how new architectural questions are framed and investigated. Their use still requires checking that their assumptions fit the target problem.
2. *Hardware modules, compiler passes, and tool wrappers* transfer conditionally, remaining viable only while their underlying invariants and interface contracts hold.
3. *Empirical performance conclusions* remain attached to the conditions that supported them. A change reopens the conclusions that depend on it; claims whose assumptions still hold need not be discarded merely because another part of the system changed.

Transferring an architectural pattern to a new target requires a dependency audit. Hardware behavior depends on compiler scheduling, memory semantics, wire parasitics, and power delivery. An unchanged register-transfer level (RTL) module can therefore behave differently in a new environment, and a learned surrogate may no longer predict the property its caller expects. The audit determines which relations need checking before reuse.

The transfer test proposed here begins with an admission check and then runs four stages (@fig-transfer-test-flow). The admission check compares the source and target decisions. If candidate boundaries, optimization objectives, constraints, acceptance criteria, comparator rules, or error costs have shifted, the decision itself is reopened. Numerical recalibration alone cannot establish that a prior conclusion answers the changed question. The four stages apply in either case, but support a new design problem when the decision has changed.

1. **Partition the source into transfer units.** Separate the source record into data, representations, methods, tool interfaces, checks, and configurations. Keep each empirical conclusion linked to the evidence and conditions that supported it.
2. **Isolate the affected slice.** Trace which dependencies and invariants the target workload, ISA, or process shift may have changed, distinguishing known violations from relations that still need checking.
3. **Assign target actions.** Designate each unit to be carried forward, updated, retrained, recalibrated, replaced, or retired.
4. **Enforce target checks and test the transfer benefit.** Requalify affected units against target references and compare decision quality and total cost with a matched target-only baseline, including the cost of adaptation and requalification.

![**Transfer testing reuses architectural components without porting unverified source conclusions.** Reusable components from a source study record are partitioned into discrete transfer units (data, representations, methods, tool interfaces, checks, and configurations), traced through changed dependencies, and assigned target actions (carry, update, retrain, recalibrate, replace, or retire) before target checks validate a new design decision. Affected claims are selectively reopened, and every interface with a changed neighbor receives an integration check while the source conclusion remains isolated.](images/fig-transfer-test-flow){#fig-transfer-test-flow width="80%" fig-alt="Transfer flow beginning at the source record, whose artifacts, methods, checks, and supported conclusion feed four stage boxes: transfer units separating data, methods, checks, and dependencies; changed dependencies tracing each material change to dependent claims and interfaces; target actions to carry, update, replace, or retire each unit; and target checks on affected units and every interface with a changed neighbor. The flow ends in a target decision box where a new comparison over target measurements supports a new conclusion. A supporting band states that components may move while the source conclusion stays attached to its source conditions and limits."}

The case for reusing an engineering artifact depends on the completeness of its dependency map and the coverage of target checks for affected claims and changed interfaces. Consider an AI-driven placement optimizer trained on one family of floorplans. A process change can alter routing resources and the relation between placement choices and final congestion. The policy might remain useful, but its source performance does not settle that question. Requalification compares its predictions or decisions with target results to establish the scope in which they can guide the new search.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Transfer Components, Not Conclusions"}
**The principle:** When adapting prior design solutions to new workloads, process nodes, or constraints, valid artifacts, tool paths, and intermediate data may carry forward.

**The application:** Before relying on a prior architectural conclusion, check whether its supporting conditions still hold in the target. Changed or uncertain dependencies require new evidence; unaffected claims can retain their source support.
:::

## Target System Shifts and Decision Reopening

A target system shift reopens prior architectural decisions whenever new workloads, silicon constraints, or interface contracts break the assumptions behind the original problem formulation. A *design problem* is the complete decision context that gives alternatives their meaning; it explicitly names candidate boundaries, target workloads, software stacks, constraints, credible comparators, and error costs. Benchmarks supply workloads, candidates represent design points, and tools observe properties, but none of these carries the full decision context in isolation. Comparing source and target determines whether we are answering the same question under changed conditions or asking a different architecture question.

Target system changes fall into three principal categories.

- **Distributional transfer.** The objective, legal actions, artifact boundary, and acceptance criteria remain stable, while the workload, operating conditions, or candidate population shift within that space (such as shifting batch sizes or input frame rates while keeping CPU ISA vector extensions or Triton compiler intermediate representation (IR) constant).
- **Component or integration transfer.** The core decision remains stable, while differences emerge in a component, interface, tool, library, or process condition along the executable or measurement path. Examples include updating a compiler backend, remapping a kernel from Arm Scalable Vector Extension operations to Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (AMX) tile operations, or altering neural processing unit (NPU) tensor dataflows. Each path needs its own supported lowering and interface checks.
- **New design problem.** The objective, legal actions, artifact boundary, or acceptance criteria change fundamentally (such as transitioning from unconstrained datacenter throughput to a strict 3\ W mobile headset power envelope).

These distinctions apply per individual claim and dependency rather than uniformly across the target. A single target change often combines these forms across distinct architectural dependencies. Selective requalification handles claims affected by distributional or component changes, whereas a new design problem forces reopening every claim tied to the changed question. The raw magnitude of a change does not dictate the response; a large workload shift may remain within the same design problem, whereas a single-line modification to an objective or action space can create a new one. Treating every workload adjustment as a new design problem wastes effort on checks whose assumptions still hold; treating a changed objective as parameter drift can preserve a conclusion that no longer answers the question.

Materiality is claim-specific. Updating a compiler toolchain reopens executable performance claims without touching RTL functional equivalence, while shifting a library operating corner reopens timing and power closure without invalidating compiler-semantics results. A change is material to a claim when it alters the candidate identity, executable path, measured quantity, objective, decision rule, ranking, constraint verdict, or underlying physical mechanism.

Every qualified component carries a *support region* (the joint set of workload, design-family, tool, library, process, interface, and version conditions under which it was originally verified). A source-to-target shift emerges whenever work qualified in one region is applied to another. As introduced in @sec-feedback-verification-trust, distribution shift captures changed data-generating conditions [@QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift] and drift tracks observed temporal variations. In architectural systems, material changes also occur across software stacks, tools, libraries, process calibrations, and hardware interfaces; these executable and measurement shifts occur even if a learned model's input distribution remains stable.

For this chapter's transfer test, generalization concerns performance on unseen cases within declared target conditions; transfer concerns reuse after a material change from source to target.[^fn-transfer-c09] Robustness concerns stability under named perturbations, faults, or attacks, which @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect measures for the complete system. The distribution-shift and requalification analysis in @sec-feedback-verification-trust determines when previously qualified evidence needs new checks.

[^fn-transfer-c09]: **Generalization vs. Transfer**: These are operational meanings for the chapter's transfer test. A study must state its source and target conditions and which changes it evaluates before either term supports an architecture claim.


Standard dataset-shift tests compare reference samples against incoming data to report divergence [@RabanserEtAl2019FailingLoudly]. In architectural evaluation, detecting a shift reopens the affected support claim immediately. The shift signal itself does not identify root causes or authorize automated adaptation; addressing it requires explicit dependency analysis and target checks.

The preliminary spatial array experiment from @sec-running-the-loop shows where those lines fall in practice. Evaluating five systolic array shapes in SCALE-Sim [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3] on a synthetic three-layer general matrix multiply (GEMM) slice, the source study found a tie under its cycle-and-utilization score and retained the 32 by 32 reference array. That no-change finding remains confined to its synthetic source context.

For a Lighthouse design considering this array as one candidate compute organization, an implementation commitment asks a different question.

> Should the 32 by 32 array, together with its compiler-visible tiling and
> memory-interface contract, be frozen for RTL implementation in the
> Lighthouse subsystem?

This shift alters the artifact boundary, acceptance criteria, and consequences of error, creating a new design problem. The isolated simulator score does not establish whether the array and its memory system can serve the Lighthouse workload within a 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) envelope. Freezing an interface constrains compiler tiling, static random-access memory (SRAM) banking, interconnect traffic, and power delivery. The target therefore needs a trace-backed workload, a compiler-generated execution path, and implementation checks that observe those costs. The retained source record contains none of those target results; the transfer application later in this chapter specifies the work still required.

## Decoupling Transfer Units Across System Boundaries

Hardware, software, and tools evolve at different rates, so a source system is partitioned before it is moved rather than transferred as a whole. Data, state, methods, tools, checks, and conclusions rarely share a single lifetime in an architecture project, and treating them as an indivisible package forces a choice between copying everything blindly and rebuilding the infrastructure entirely. Naming the units separately is what makes a source-to-target comparison actionable, because each unit can then carry its own dependency and its own check.

### Automated Dependency Mapping and Invariant Extraction

Every transfer unit carries an *invariant* (a core relation that must remain true across both source and target for the unit to retain its meaning). Some invariants appear in interface specifications; others are implicit in the implementation. A proposed capability for an AI-native design system is to combine execution logs, source analysis, and environment metadata into a dependency graph, then identify assumptions that a target change might break. A language model could propose missing relations for checking, but the graph would remain incomplete wherever the source record omitted a dependency. Automatic extraction therefore needs validation against independently specified interfaces and known dependency changes before it can guide selective requalification. For each known change, reviewers would identify the units and claims expected to be affected independently of the generated map, then check whether the map reaches them. A missed dependency would require correcting the map and widening the requalification scope; recovering the known cases would support its use without establishing completeness.

Consider an illustrative cache controller that consumes SRAM data two cycles after issuing a request. A target macro that returns data after three cycles breaks that fixed-latency invariant unless the controller implements a ready/valid handshake or credit-based flow control. Static analysis and a generated SystemVerilog assertion could help expose the mismatch. The verification task is to check that the assertion captures the intended request–response behavior, that the target macro model represents the changed latency, and that the property is exercised rather than passing vacuously. A failed check would block reuse of the controller under the old assumption. A passing generated assertion alone would not establish that all implicit timing assumptions had been found.

Transfer units should be scoped to the smallest versioned boundary possessing a declared interface or invariant, provided an independently meaningful target check applies. If a dependency cannot be isolated with such a check, it must remain in the same unit. Consider an LLVM IR module lowered through a backend supporting RISC-V Vector (RVV) or x86 AVX-512, or a Triton kernel compiled for a separately declared, supported target. The compiler toolchain and generated binary can be treated as separate units only when their identities and inputs are fixed and the binary receives an independent check for the claimed property, such as semantic equivalence for behavior or an ABI check for interface compatibility. Otherwise, the compiler-to-binary lowering path must be transferred and checked together.

The transfer map puts the four stages into practice, naming the action a broken dependency permits and the target check that action requires (@tbl-ch9-transfer-map). Down every row, a single target shift demands tailored, unit-specific actions rather than a uniform reuse policy. Each action pairs with a domain-specific check on held-out tasks or hardware references; the resulting evidence supports reuse only within the conditions and properties checked. For learned components, *held-out* means target tasks kept apart from fitting or calibration.

| **Transfer unit** | **Changed dependency** | **Valid action** | **Required target check** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Data, records, and current knowledge** | Workload, design space, objectives, provenance, collection conditions, specifications, manuals, libraries, or project documents differ. | Reuse the historical record; refresh target data and sources; retire stale sources; narrow unsupported coverage. | Check trace and artifact provenance, source identity and version, target coverage and exclusions, source-to-target overlap, and whether retrieved material supports the target fact. |
| **Representation and project state** | Constraints, interfaces, artifact versions, or cross-layer relationships differ. | Refresh live state; adapt the representation; replace a representation that hides a required relationship. | Check schema and constraint completeness, version consistency, and integration with neighboring state. |
| **Learned component** | Training support, inputs, outputs, objectives, constraints, project facts, or data-generating conditions changed. | Requalify the unchanged component; rerun a generator or optimizer; recalibrate a numerical mapping; adapt, retrain, replace, or retire the component when needed. | Test every role it fills on held-out target tasks, including accuracy or calibration, candidate legality, objective quality, stale knowledge, failure classes, and performance against the declared comparator. |
| **Conventional method** | Analytical assumptions, solver formulation, design space, or objective changed. | Reuse, adapt, rerun, replace, or retire the method. | Check its assumptions on the target and compare its target result with the same decision rule used for other methods. |
| **Tool interface and environment component** | Command syntax, parameter meaning, output schema, status codes, tool or library version, constraint and configuration files, random seed, license, runtime, machine resource, reset behavior, or isolation changed. | Refresh configuration; adapt, replace, or retire the component; rerun affected work. | Check target-version execution, interface parsing and failure classification, constraints and stochastic state, reset and isolation behavior, resource accounting, and integration with connected tools. |
| **Empirical screening check** | Target coverage, observed conditions, error tolerance, or relationship to the target reference changed. | Requalify before reuse; recalibrate only when a numerical mapping or threshold changes; adapt, rerun, replace, or retire the check. | Measure target support and class-specific errors against a separate reference capable of observing the property at risk. |
| **Formal, equivalence, deterministic, or rule-based check** | The target specification, assumptions, properties, representation relation, rules, or tool version changed. | Review the specification mapping; requalify the target setup; adapt, rerun, replace, or retire the check. | Check property and assumption coverage, the relation being established, target tool integration, and known positive, negative, and inconclusive cases. |
| **Routing or escalation policy** | Check cost, consequence, qualified coverage, or available review capacity changed. | Adapt, replace, narrow, or retire the policy. | Exercise routing thresholds, uncertain cases, failure injection, escalation, and resource limits on the target. |
| **Configured system** | Any neighboring component or interface changed, even when this configuration did not. | Rerun target integration; recompose, adapt, replace, narrow, or reject the configuration when required. | Repeat the end-to-end target task with pinned versions, total product-path costs, failures, and a credible alternative. |
| **Architecture and contribution conclusions** | The target decision, comparator, budget, or measured path differs from the source. | Narrow the conclusion to its supported source scope or reject its transfer. | Repeat the architecture comparison and the matched contribution comparison under target conditions. |
: **Transfer decisions are component-specific.** A unit moves only by assigning an action suited to the broken dependency, paired with a target check observing the resulting architectural risk. {#tbl-ch9-transfer-map tbl-colwidths="[20,28,24,28]"}

A conclusion is never updated mechanically; it is narrowed to the conditions the target still satisfies or rejected outright, and rejection preserves the historical record while keeping stale evidence out of the new decision.

*Negative transfer* occurs when a transferred or adapted method performs worse on the target than a clean target-only alternative [@WangEtAl2019NegativeTransfer]. In computer architecture, evaluating negative transfer requires comparing overall decision quality and total methodology cost. Claiming a transfer benefit demands a matched target-only comparison where both arms receive identical tasks, budgets, and stopping rules, with the target-only arm starting without source priors. Both arms need comparable opportunities to tune on the target; an untuned target-only baseline can make reuse appear beneficial. Total cost accounting must include adaptation, requalification, and integration overhead alongside execution time, including physical checks when the target claim requires them.

Transfer also needs an economic justification. Partitioning a source record, tracing dependencies, requalifying carried units, and integrating them with changed neighbors all consume effort. A fresh target study has costs of its own, including rebuilding tools and collecting data that the source may already provide. Reopening the architecture decision therefore does not settle whether reuse is worthwhile. A source conclusion may no longer apply while its simulator wrapper or workload-processing code remains expensive to reproduce.

The useful comparison is between adaptation and requalification costs on one side and rebuilding costs on the other, at comparable decision quality. Before committing the full budget, a limited transfer study can estimate which units are worth carrying; the matched target-only arm then tests the claimed benefit. If source priors worsen the decision or cost more than they save, they should be retired. Qualified tools and historical records may still be reused. Starting without a source prior is a defensible outcome, but it need not mean starting without reusable infrastructure.

### Isolating Design Slices

Dependency tracking isolates the affected slice of a configured system. The goal is to requalify claims that depend on changed conditions, paired with targeted integration checks wherever affected components meet unchanged neighbors. An incomplete dependency map can miss part of that slice, which is why invariant extraction needs the checks described above. For instance, an NPU tensor dataflow shift (such as moving from weight-stationary to output-stationary tile scheduling) forces re-evaluating timing and memory power without altering compiler-level language semantics.

The actions apply differently to each unit type. Retraining changes a learned component; recalibration adjusts a numerical mapping or threshold. Data and representations are updated, while a tool interface may need a configuration update, an adaptation, or replacement. For example, in a congestion predictor trained on prior routed designs, learned weights and feature schemas form the transferable artifact, while placed netlists and process libraries constitute target inputs. Reusing the predictor requires checking schema compatibility and class-specific error bounds on held-out routed target designs. Those checks determine whether unchanged weights suffice or further adaptation is needed.

Machine-learning work on distribution shift and hidden dependencies [@WangEtAl2019NegativeTransfer; @QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift; @SculleyEtAl2015Hidden] motivates checking interactions as well as individual components. A subsystem optimized in isolation can impose new costs on the system it joins. In hardware, those costs may appear in global interconnect and clock distribution, outside the boundary of the block-level report.

::: {.callout-failure-mode title="Local Optimization Can Increase System Cost"}
**The trap.** An optimizer reduces isolated accelerator-block power, and the block-level improvement is treated as a system-level saving.

**The mechanism.** In this constructed illustration, the revised block layout requires longer global interconnect and more clock-distribution power after integration into the system-on-chip (SoC). The local saving is outweighed by costs outside the optimizer's measurement boundary.

| Metric | Unoptimized Baseline | Locally Optimized Blocks |
|:---|---:|---:|
| Accelerator Block Power (Local) | 120\ mW | 80\ mW |
| Network-on-Chip Router Power | 40\ mW | 70\ mW |
| Top-Level Clock Distribution | 30\ mW | 60\ mW |
| Global Interconnect Routing | 10\ mm | 25\ mm |
| **Total System Power (Aggregated)** | **190\ mW** | **210\ mW** |

: **Illustrative integration overhead.** These constructed values show how lower isolated block power can be outweighed by higher interconnect and clock power; they are not measurements of an implemented system.

**The lesson.** Bound optimization and transfer checks to the smallest enclosing architectural boundary that captures the relevant interconnect, clock, and thermal coupling. A local improvement supports a system claim only after those added costs are included.
:::

When a change affects connections between blocks, an enclosing-boundary check must measure those integration costs. The block can remain a transfer unit for properties checked independently, while its system-power claim requires the wider measurement.

### Validating Transfer Conditions

Checks required by the transfer map establish different kinds of assurance. A formal proof establishes stated properties under specific assumptions; an equivalence check establishes a defined relation between representations; deterministic analysis computes quantities under the assumptions of its model and inputs; and rule-based heuristics provide repeatability without proof of correctness. Passing target regressions supports the tool-integration behavior exercised by those tests, but does not expand formal property coverage or validate heuristic soundness (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). When a neighboring component changes a dependency relevant to the transfer claim, integration checks must cover that change even if the module itself is untouched. For example, a wrapper may parse simulator syntax correctly while receiving invalid parameters from a revised representation.

Decomposing proposal, checking, and integration into separate components makes responsibilities inspectable. However, this structure alone does not create independent evidence if the components share underlying models, context, training data, or tools. Distinct toolchains or information paths can expose different failures, but shared assumptions can still produce shared blind spots; independence must be assessed for the property being checked (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). Furthermore, component qualification does not automatically compose; localized changes often disrupt overall system behavior in ways that block-level metrics fail to detect [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden]. Dependency-specific checks therefore need end-to-end integration tests where the claim depends on interactions between components. When evidence spans multiple fidelities, those tests must address the physical constraints relevant to the target claim before an irreversible tapeout commitment. Carrying out and acting on these checks also requires active tool access, up-to-date operating knowledge, engineer veto rights, and the instrumentation necessary to challenge anomalous tool returns (@sec-what-architect-owns).

## Transfer Under Distribution Shift

Applying the transfer map to the array study exposes properties the source study left unsettled (@tbl-ch9-source-target). Moving from cycle-level simulation toward physical silicon also reopens the architecture decision. A local no-change recommendation does not establish that the array and its interfaces satisfy implementation constraints. The prospective target below creates new obligations for workload coverage, integration checks, and fallbacks. Each row connects a changed condition to the work it requires; the target checks are proposed, not executed results.

| **Condition** | **Executed array study** | **Implementation-facing target** | **Obligation created by the change** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Result cost and delay | Retained seconds-scale cycle-level simulator outputs and an inspectable replay path; no independent replay or validation result is retained | Compiler experiments (LLVM, Triton), RTL synthesis, floorplanning, and routed checks | Screening uses simulators (SCALE-Sim, gem5, Verilator) and budgets for slower downstream checks and review time. |
| Reversibility | A simulated shape can be discarded | An array and interface freeze creates downstream software and hardware rework | The 32 by 32 array remains provisional with a preserved fallback until target checks settle. |
| Coupling and interface span | Array dimensions varied while mapping and interfaces stayed fixed | Compiler mapping, RVV extensions, SRAM, NPU dataflow interconnect, host, and accelerator contracts interact | Measure the executable software path alongside end-to-end offload cost. |
| Observability and check independence | Cycles, utilization, and modeled word traffic from one simulator | Correctness, latency, bandwidth, area, timing, congestion, power, thermal behavior, reliability, and security properties required by the target | Add memory-system, RTL, implementation, thermal, fault, and security checks where target consequences demand them, disclosing shared assumptions. |
| Consequence | A local no-change recommendation | A 3\ W subsystem commitment affecting later implementation | Replace local scores with comprehensive target criteria, explicitly stating untested properties. |
| Workload | Synthetic three-layer GEMM slice | Trace-backed spatial-tracking distribution, including tails and drift | Rebuild workload coverage rather than treating the source slice as broadly representative. |
| Software turnover | One frozen mapping and tool configuration | Compiler and runtime versions (Triton, LLVM) continue to evolve | Version hardware and software together, rerunning affected claims when snapshots update. |
: **Changed conditions accumulate test obligations.** The target study retains the source record, but cannot inherit the source conclusion. {#tbl-ch9-source-target tbl-colwidths="[20,24,26,30]"}

A transfer-risk decomposition models *false acceptance* (accepting a transferred candidate for an RTL freeze when full target evidence would reject it). The expected loss attributable to false acceptance equals its probability multiplied by the expected loss of reversal, rework, and permanent errors conditional on that acceptance. Workload mismatches, limited observability, and uncalibrated proxies increase the probability of false acceptance; tighter interface coupling, downstream commitments, and system consequences amplify conditional loss. Complete decisions must balance false acceptance against false rejection, missed performance, and requalification costs.

Workload evaluation requires decoupling inherent workload properties from single-machine artifacts [@HosteEeckhout2007MICA], specifying trace-backed distributions, common and tail execution shapes, and versioned compiler stacks. Mapping semantics must be bound explicitly across compiler paths (Triton grid parameters, LLVM vector bounds) and simulator configurations (SCALE-Sim, gem5). Compiler searches such as AutoTVM and Ansor evaluate tensor-program implementations on particular hardware targets [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @ZhengEtAl2020Ansor].

Transitioning to RTL and physical implementation shifts observable properties and reversal costs. Compiler-generated tests and simulation yield behavioral evidence; formal property verification establishes properties within declared model bounds; equivalence checking verifies representation mappings without proving architectural intent; and synthesis and place-and-route produce netlists, layouts, and estimates for timing, area, and congestion. Electrothermal behavior requires dedicated analysis with workload activity, power-delivery models, packaging, and thermal boundary conditions. Signoff additionally requires tools, models, and checks qualified for the target process. At scaled semiconductor nodes, increasing global-wire delay relative to logic gates makes extracted post-layout verification essential [@HoMaiHorowitz2001FutureOfWires].

The target checks become easier to choose when each shift is tied to the relation it can break. Five examples connect the transfer map to concrete architectural mechanisms, from the order in which a core observes writes to the energy spent moving data between packages:

1. **Cross-ISA and memory consistency shifts.** Synchronization code can depend on ordering that the target ISA does not preserve. Consider message passing: a producer writes a payload and then a flag; a consumer observes the flag and then reads the payload. Under a relaxed model such as RISC-V Weak Memory Ordering (RVWMO), the implementation needs the appropriate synchronization to preserve those relationships [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]. For ordinary memory accesses, producer-side `fence w, w` and consumer-side `fence r, r` illustrate the ordering obligations. Source-language atomics and compiler lowering must preserve them too. The invariant is visibility of the payload when the consumer observes the flag, not the survival of the same instruction sequence. RVWMO remains multi-copy atomic,[^fn-multicopy-relaxed-c09] so weak ordering must not be confused with arbitrary write propagation. Target litmus tests should exercise the particular ordering relation the module needs.
2. **Vector architecture shifts.** Fixed-width single instruction, multiple data (SIMD) kernels often encode a particular number of elements per iteration and a separate cleanup path. RISC-V Vector (RVV 1.0) supports vector-length-agnostic loops in which `vsetvli` selects an active element count from the remaining work and the vector configuration [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA]. A strip-mining loop advances by the returned count, allowing the algorithm to run across supported vector lengths. The transfer unit is therefore the algorithm together with its lowering assumptions, not necessarily the original machine-code loop. Requalification checks numerical behavior and boundary cases under the target vector configuration; performance measurements then determine whether the adapted loop uses the target efficiently.
3. **Physical transistor node shifts.** Floorplan heuristics and wire-parasitic surrogates depend on the process libraries and routing stack used to qualify them. A move from a frontside power grid to a backside power delivery network (BSPDN)[^fn-bspdn-c09] changes where power is routed and how signal-routing resources are shared. The transferable object may be the netlist representation or prediction method, while its fitted delay and congestion relationships require target evidence. The practical check is to compare predictions with extracted target layouts and separately examine power delivery and thermal behavior. A node name alone does not establish either failure or successful transfer.
4. **Workload paradigm shifts.** Dense matrix multiplication gives a systolic array regular tiles and opportunities for spatial data reuse. Mixture-of-experts workloads introduce token-dependent routing across experts, which can change tile sizes and the distribution of work. Autoregressive decoding also requires reading the key-value (KV) cache[^fn-kvcache-c09] as tokens are generated. Those changes can increase memory demand relative to useful array work, but their effect depends on batching, mapping, and the memory system. The transfer check therefore reruns representative target traces and measures both utilization and traffic. Low utilization would motivate a different mapping or data-movement mechanism; it would not, by itself, prove that the array must be replaced.
5. **Interconnect and bandwidth density shifts.** Changing physical reach changes the link model that a transferred design needs. Channel loss and SerDes[^fn-serdes-c09] equalization can increase the energy spent crossing package and board boundaries, while short die-to-die links use different signaling and packaging assumptions. Bandwidth density, energy per bit, and reach therefore need to be compared under explicit interface conditions.

[^fn-multicopy-relaxed-c09]: **Multi-Copy Atomicity**: Once a store is visible to another hart, it is conceptually visible to all harts. This property does not require every pair of a hart's memory operations to preserve program order [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA].

[^fn-bspdn-c09]: **BSPDN (Backside Power Delivery Network)**: An arrangement that routes power through the backside of the silicon wafer, separating part of the power-delivery network from frontside signal routing. Its resistance and routing benefits depend on the implemented network and its connections to the devices.

[^fn-kvcache-c09]: **KV-cache**: In transformer models, the Key-Value cache stores the previously computed key and value tensors for past tokens so they do not need to be recomputed. During autoregressive generation, reading these tensors can make attention bandwidth-intensive; whether that traffic limits generation depends on context length, batch size, model architecture, and the implementation.

[^fn-serdes-c09]: **SerDes (Serializer/Deserializer)**: A functional block used in high-speed communications to convert parallel data to serial data and vice-versa, essential for pushing data across lossy long-distance electrical links but increasingly power-hungry at high speeds.

The provisional values in @fig-interconnect-scaling have unresolved source support and require target-specific specification or measurement checks before they can guide a transferred design.

Wafer-scale integration (@fig-cerebras-wse) reduces chip-boundary crossings for traffic kept on the wafer. Co-packaged optics (CPO) offers a different way to carry traffic beyond the package, with its own packaging and thermal constraints. In either case, transferring an accelerator requires identifying which boundaries its workload traffic actually crosses.

Start with representative target traces and identify the traffic crossing each die, package, and board boundary. For each crossing, measure the transferred volume and its timing, then compare the resulting bandwidth demand with what the target link can sustain under the intended conditions. State which endpoint and link components are included in the energy measurement and how bandwidth density is normalized. For example, a proposed mapping that keeps intermediate results on a wafer should be checked for the crossings it removes and for the input and output traffic that still leaves the wafer. A link-level improvement supports a system-level efficiency claim only after the remaining crossings and their costs are included.

![**The Cerebras Wafer-Scale Engine (WSE).** The processor uses a 300\ mm silicon wafer to keep communication on one integrated substrate that would otherwise cross chip boundaries. Its physical form illustrates why an interconnect cost model must identify which boundaries a workload's traffic actually crosses.](images/cerebras_wse.jpg){#fig-cerebras-wse width="90%" fig-alt="A large, square, copper-colored silicon processor being held by gloved hands, demonstrating its massive size compared to traditional chips."}

![**Provisional interconnect comparison.** Transcribed values have unresolved provenance. Selected die-to-die entries, including Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express (UCIe) and Bunch of Wires, approach or exceed $1.0\ \text{Tbps/mm}$ with energy below $0.7\ \text{pJ/bit}$; NVLink 4/5 and PCIe Gen 5/6 use $4\text{--}10\ \text{pJ/bit}$. Reach descriptions of $\le 25\ \text{mm}$ for die-to-die links, $500\text{--}1{,}000\ \text{mm}$ for package/board links, and $>10\ \text{m}$ for optics are absent from the dataset. UCIe and earlier NVLink sources [@UCIeConsortium2026Spec; @FoleyDanskin2017Pascal] do not validate the full compilation. Target-specific checks are required.](images/plot_ch9.png){#fig-interconnect-scaling width="85%" fig-alt="Log-log scatter plot of bandwidth density versus energy efficiency comparing die-to-die, package-scale, and board/optical interconnect standards."}

These examples require different actions because the affected units differ. A synchronization module may need fences and target litmus tests.[^fn-litmus-c09] A fixed-width kernel may need a new vector lowering while retaining its algorithm. A process-dependent surrogate first needs requalification; adaptation or retraining follows only if its errors warrant it. A workload shift reopens the array's utilization claim, while a change in interconnect reach calls for a cost model of the links actually used. The map helps choose among those actions without declaring every source artifact obsolete.

[^fn-litmus-c09]: **Litmus Tests**: In memory consistency, litmus tests are small concurrent programs used to verify ordering rules. For example, testing whether RISC-V `amo.aq` (acquire) and `amo.rl` (release) modifiers correctly enforce visibility across harts.

The measurement boundary also determines which physical conclusions a check can support. Timing closure in OpenSTA or Cadence Tempus establishes that the analyzed paths meet their timing constraints under the specified process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) corners and modeling assumptions.[^fn-pvt-c09] It does not independently establish dynamic $IR$-drop,[^fn-irdrop-c09] electromigration, spatial thermal hotspots, or total power under a real workload, so the thermal question the node shift raises stays open after the timing report closes. Lower reversibility then demands explicit containment (bypasses, disables, guardbands, spare cells) tested against credible failure classes before an irreversible physical commitment is made.

[^fn-pvt-c09]: **PVT corners**: Process, voltage, and temperature corners are specified combinations used to analyze circuit behavior. Timing closure establishes that the analyzed paths meet their timing constraints under the selected corners and modeling assumptions; it does not establish every functional, power-delivery, or thermal property of the chip.

[^fn-irdrop-c09]: **$IR$-drop**: The voltage drop across the power delivery network due to wire resistance ($V = I \times R$). Excessive $IR$-drop reduces the supply voltage reaching transistors, which slows down logic gates and can cause timing or functional failures.

::: {.callout-war-story title="A correction must reach the physical failure"}
**The claim.** In January 2011, Intel disclosed a design error in the Cougar Point chipset shipping with Sandy Bridge platforms, stating consumers could safely continue using affected systems while manufacturers arranged a permanent solution [@Intel2011CougarPoint].

**The gap.** The underlying silicon defect caused specific SATA ports to physically degrade over time. Intel halted shipments and taped out corrected silicon rather than attempting a software-only fix.

**The lesson.** A permanent correction demanded revised silicon alongside costly repair or replacement programs. Containment and correction mechanisms succeed only if they reach the physical component and intercept the exact failure mode threatening the target system.
:::
## Version Dependencies and Interface Contracts

Software turnover, the last row of @tbl-ch9-source-target, can change a result even when the hardware remains fixed. The offload economics that @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales works out with the LogCA model[^fn-logca-rem-c09] relate an accelerator's break-even point to communication latency, host overhead, workload granularity, host computation, and acceleration. The host runtime and compiler decide where a workload sits relative to that point, by fusing operations into payloads large enough to amortize invocation overhead and by eliminating the off-chip intermediate allocations that pull operational intensity below the link's balance point. A transferred offload result therefore carries a compiler version inside it. Move the kernel to a target whose compiler fuses less, and the same accelerator can land on the wrong side of break-even with no hardware change at all. An isolated kernel speedup becomes a transferred result only when compiler-generated code executes on the target under a pinned toolchain, with numerics, memory-ordering semantics, application binary interfaces (ABIs), and device contracts preserved, which is why the software path is a transfer unit in its own right (@tbl-ch9-transfer-map).

[^fn-logca-rem-c09]: **LogCA Model**: The parameters represent Latency, Overhead, Granularity, Computational Index, and Acceleration. Together they estimate break-even points for hardware offload under the model's assumptions.


The version pair identifies the conditions under which a hardware–software result was measured. Changing an NPU array geometry or a compiler lowering pass may alter the executed schedule even when the source program stays fixed. Cross-layer optimizations, such as memory-aware algorithmic tiling (FlashAttention [@DaoEtAl2022FlashAttention]) and narrow numerical formats (Microscaling / MX formats [@RouhaniEtAl2023Microscaling]), make that dependence concrete. Requalification follows the affected latency, bandwidth, accuracy, or efficiency claim; a version change is a reason to inspect its dependencies, not evidence that every invariant has failed.

Because software tuning cycles outpace hardware implementation checks, the two must co-evolve without allowing fast software iterations to overwrite slower hardware baselines. Fast software results can propose hardware revisions, but those revisions enter versioned target state only through a shared study record and explicit authorization. This structure decouples development velocity without sacrificing provenance. Software state encompasses compilers, runtimes, programming interfaces, drivers, and generated binaries; comparisons with an earlier baseline require restoring the compatible dependency versions that produced it, rather than assuming an isolated binary recreates the earlier system.

MLCommons MLPerf datacenter submissions provide a setting for measuring this coupling [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf; @ReddiEtAl2020MLPerfInference]. The retained compilation in @fig-ch09-mlperf-software-dividend is provisional. Its rows have not been reconciled against individual benchmark submissions, and its hardware/software bars select separate maxima across workloads. It therefore cannot establish a matched generational comparison. Published software optimizations motivate testing whether maturation changes a hardware comparison [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware; @DaoEtAl2022FlashAttention]; that test must hold workload, system scale, result definition, and measurement window fixed enough for the intended claim.

Suppose an architect compares a generated hardware candidate using an immature compiler backend with a production baseline that benefits from years of operator fusion. The end-to-end measurement may be useful as a comparison of the two available systems, but it does not isolate their microarchitectures. Pinning hardware revisions and compiler snapshots identifies the configurations being compared; reproducing the experiment also requires its inputs, procedures, and measurement conditions. Attribution requires an additional comparison that examines software effects, such as tuning both candidates under matched budgets or perturbing tile sizes to test whether one result depends on a favorable compiler schedule. A frozen toolchain preserves that interaction; it does not remove it.

![**Provisional software and hardware comparison.** Labeled 2018–2026, this compilation ends in April 2025 and remains unreconciled with individual MLPerf submissions. (a) NVIDIA V100, A100, H100, and Google Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) v4 series contain $1.3\times\text{--}3.8\times$ multipliers over 12 to 24 months. (b) Volta through Blackwell hardware-step ratios span $1.2\times\text{--}7.2\times$; software-dividend values span $1.0\times\text{--}3.8\times$. Bars use separate per-platform maxima across workloads, not matched pairs. Cited methods and optimization accounts [@MattsonEtAl2020MLPerf; @EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware; @DaoEtAl2022FlashAttention] do not validate these values or a general software/hardware relationship.](images/fig-ch09-mlperf-software-dividend){#fig-ch09-mlperf-software-dividend width="80%" fig-alt="Two-panel provisional compilation of MLPerf-related values, not yet reconciled with individual submissions. (a) Transcribed multipliers from 1.3x to 3.82x over 12 to 24 months for V100, A100, TPU v4, and H100. (b) Hardware-step and software-dividend bars from Volta through Blackwell use separate per-platform maxima across workloads, so they are not matched comparisons."}

Deployment observations motivate calibration studies for subsequent hardware generations, but cannot automatically update surrogate models or design rules due to predictive uncertainty degradation under dataset shift [@OvadiaEtAl2019UncertaintyShift]. Calibration studies must bind observations to shipped hardware, exact software stacks, workload cohorts, and measurement conditions, separating calibration samples from held-out validation sets. For example, NVIDIA's reported $17\%$ BERT optimization on identical H100 hardware between MLPerf Training v2.1 and v3.0 reflects software enablement rather than a revised hardware baseline [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware].

## Cross-Stack Pattern Transfer

For the Lighthouse transfer, we can now assign work to the dependencies exposed earlier. The target remains prospective. The retained array sweep has not been extended into an implementation-facing study. Its admission check already identified a new design problem, because freezing the array and its interfaces carries consequences that the source simulator score cannot assess. The four stages specify how reusable source material could support that new study.

1. **Partition the source into transfer units.** Separate the source study into historical records, workload definitions, project state representations, proposing methods, the SCALE-Sim screen, tool interfaces, candidate artifacts, and conclusions.
2. **Isolate the affected slice.** Trace changes across workload distributions, compiler mappings, executable paths, process libraries, physical checks, and power targets. Source simulator outputs serve as historical data but do not provide implementation evidence.
3. **Assign target actions.** Preserve historical artifacts, update workload and project state, and requalify the screen against target references. Adapt interfaces or recalibrate the screen only where checks identify a need. Keep the source recommendation confined to its original scope.
4. **Enforce target checks and test transfer benefits.** Pair every changed dependency with a target check observing its specific risk, with integration checks at component boundaries. Validate claimed transfer benefits against matched target-only baselines.

The test structures the study but does not authorize an array or interface freeze; until legal target candidate sets and credible comparators are declared, the target decision remains open.

Two units show why the actions differ. The SCALE-Sim wrapper and the five candidate identities can be retained for reuse. A rerun under the pinned source configuration would test whether the wrapper reproduces the retained cycle and utilization counts. That check is still pending; even a successful rerun would qualify source-study execution, not the wrapper's ability to predict Lighthouse power.

The source decision rule has a different limit. Its ratio of cycles to utilization omits the memory traffic that the simulator also modeled (@sec-running-the-loop). Word traffic matters to the target because moving each word consumes energy, but traffic counts alone do not establish power. The target needs an energy model, execution rates, and the rest of the subsystem budget before it can test the 3\ W constraint. The source score therefore cannot admit any shape for implementation, including the retained 32 by 32 reference. This is an unresolved target decision, not evidence that all five shapes fail.

An automated transfer harness that carries the source comparator forward could incorrectly describe the reference array as power-qualified. The error would be an unsupported power conclusion, not a demonstrated 3\ W violation. A memory-aware target comparison might retain that array, choose another, or reject every candidate. Keeping those outcomes open is what permits the source artifacts to help without letting the source verdict decide a different problem.

Reuse also need not freeze the source design space. If the target study permits changes to the compute organization, the system can generate alternative hardware and software designs and use evaluation to guide redesign. Each alternative then brings its own mapping, memory-interface, and implementation checks; retaining the source wrapper does not exempt a new organization from those obligations.

Target obligations pair minimum tests with explicit claim boundaries (@tbl-ch9-target-tests), and an obligation left untested stays out of every generalized claim.

| **Target obligation** | **Minimum test** | **Boundary if absent** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Workload coverage** | Trace-backed common and tail cases, strictly versioned with all exclusions declared. | No representativeness claim. |
| **Candidate comparison** | Predeclared legal target space, search/evaluation budgets, credible comparator, decision rule, and sensitivity check. | No claims outside evaluated candidates; no comparative AI-contribution claim if arms cannot be distinguished. |
| **Transfer benefit** | Matched comparison against a target-only arm sharing tasks, data, tool access, budgets, and stopping rules, accounting for adaptation, requalification, integration, and retirement costs. | Forfeit transfer-benefit claim. Harmful priors must be retired; cost-neutral priors retained only if improving another declared criterion. |
| **Mapping and software path** | Compiler-generated end-to-end execution with a declared, supported backend for each path (such as LLVM/RVV, or Triton where a target backend is available), using pinned mappings, compilers, runtimes, ISA configurations, and interfaces. | Cannot claim array is usable by the target software stack. |
| **Interface and memory cost** | Measure offload granularity, bandwidth, traffic, and latency on the target or a qualified reference path; use LogCA and Roofline to interpret performance limits, with calibrated energy models capturing execution rates, duty cycles, leakage, and subsystem boundaries. | Forfeit 3\ W power or system-speedup claims. |
| **Cheap-screen validity** | Check representative target samples against a reference able to observe the screened property, enforcing class-specific error limits, uncertainty measures, and drift audits. Models such as gem5 or Verilator may support functional or cycle-level checks within their scope; physical and energy claims need suitable implementation or calibrated energy references. | SCALE-Sim serves as a source study tool rather than a valid target decision filter. |
| **RTL behavior** | Independently derived reference tests, linting, functional simulation (Verilator), synthesis (Yosys), formal property verification (JasperGold / SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA)), and target-specific fault/threat models. | No implementation-readiness, reliability, or security claims beyond checked properties. |
| **Physical behavior** | Pin the 3\ nm-class low-power process design kit (PDK), libraries, and PVT corners. Establish target support before selecting implementation and timing tools, such as OpenROAD or OpenSTA; check setup/hold corners, congestion, dynamic/leakage power, and electrothermal behavior with the required analysis flows (such as Ansys RedHawk-SC Electrothermal). | No physical-feasibility claim beyond checked conditions. Signoff and tapeout require a separately qualified foundry flow. |
| **Containment** | Exercise bypasses, disable functions, guardbands, isolation mechanisms, and fallbacks against specific target faults or attacks. | Cannot claim implementation will contain or recover from failure. |
| **Operational readiness** | Confirm tool access, engineer veto rights and instrumentation to challenge anomalous tool returns, and recorded decision authority. | Cannot claim transferred workflow is operable, challengeable, or capable of supporting commitment. |
: **Target obligations define required measurements.** Untested boundaries remain explicit in the architectural record. {#tbl-ch9-target-tests tbl-colwidths="[25,45,30]"}

The cheap-screen row separates executable reuse from predictive validity. A cheap screen such as SCALE-Sim transfers as an empirical check, never as a verdict. Its validated coverage on the target, the share of comparisons it settles within declared error against a reference that can observe the property at risk, is measured anew, and the screening economics that @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization works out apply only to that target-measured coverage.

Three representative scenarios illustrate how the transfer test scales across physical design, software optimization, and silicon failure (@tbl-ch9-transfer-stress-tests): a physical-design case (learned congestion prediction across shifting PDKs using CircuitNet [@ChaiEtAl2022CircuitNet] and ChiPBench [@WangEtAl2025ChiPBench]), vendor-reported software optimization (NVIDIA H100 MLPerf results [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware]), and physical silicon defects (Intel Cougar Point SATA degradation [@Intel2011CougarPoint]).

| **Transfer unit** | **Changed dependency** | **Valid action** | **Required target check** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Learned congestion predictor trained on specific process, library, and design family** | Target process, standard-cell library, netlist family, placement flow, or routed-result definition shifts. | Requalify unchanged predictor; recalibrate, adapt, retrain, or retire only after isolating what fails. | Measure class-specific target errors and decision quality against held-out routed target results. |
| **H100 software optimization results across MLPerf Training v2.1/v3.0** [@EassaEryilmaz2023H100MLPerfSoftware] | Subsequent compiler (Triton, LLVM), library, workload, or hardware generation alters configuration. | Constrain published improvement to reported versions/workloads; rerun comparison for new pair. | Repeat end-to-end workload measurement, pinning hardware and software versions under identical result definitions. |
| **Cougar Point containment and correction results** [@Intel2011CougarPoint] | Target defect and remediation mechanisms differ. Intel required revised silicon and replacement programs. | For the reported SATA-degradation defect, distinguish temporary containment from the revised silicon needed for permanent correction. | Exercise corrected silicon and containment strategies against the target failure class before claiming correction. |
: **Transfer tests apply across learned, software, and physical components.** Actions follow changed dependencies, and target checks observe specific claimed failures or improvements. {#tbl-ch9-transfer-stress-tests tbl-colwidths="[22,26,24,28]"}

Transferring components does not alter decision rights. Automated systems propose or screen candidates within declared studies, while named architects and reviewers remain responsible for freezes, waivers, signoffs, and tapeout decisions (@sec-what-architect-owns). The source study structure and reference candidate can support target exploration, while the original source conclusion remains attached to the conditions that established it.

## Open Questions

Transferring architectural patterns across workloads, compiler toolchains, and semiconductor process nodes depends on identifying which invariants survive the move. Four open questions follow from that dependence.

- **How can a transfer study bound the risk of silently discarding its best candidates?** Requalifying a screening surrogate on target samples does not reveal every candidate it wrongly rejects. Under workload or technology shift, false rejections can remove viable architectures from the search without producing an error flag. Active sampling and audits of randomly selected rejected candidates offer ways to expose the problem, using a reference that can observe the property being screened. What remains unresolved is how to allocate those audits and bound missed opportunity when the search itself changes which candidates reach the filter.

- **When does a hardware advantage survive a change in compiler scheduling?** A pinned compiler preserves the scheduling choices that interact with each candidate. An accelerator may beat its baseline because its tensor dimensions divide evenly into the compiler's loop tiles, so the gain belongs to an alignment between one array shape and one scheduler. The unresolved question is how much sensitivity testing or candidate-specific schedule optimization is sufficient for the intended hardware claim. Perturbing tile sizes and problem dimensions can expose a fragile win, but a finite set of probes cannot establish independence from every future compiler choice.

- **Which parts of a graph-based physical predictor remain useful across process nodes?** The transfer map distinguishes a reusable representation from its fitted numerical relationships. A netlist graph can preserve connectivity while target libraries, routing resources, and pin-access rules change how that structure maps to delay or congestion. The unresolved issue is whether representations that separate these dependencies can reduce target-data needs without hiding rare physical failures. Comparisons with target-only training must examine the resulting design decisions as well as predictive error, because an improvement in average accuracy may still leave harmful screening errors.

- **How can a transfer system establish which timing claims a floorplan change leaves intact?** Selective requalification depends on identifying every affected dependency, while a macro move can change wire loads or clock relationships beyond that macro. Incremental timing analysis can update a known timing graph [@OpenROADDocs]; the transfer problem is deciding whether that graph, extracted parasitics, and interface assumptions still cover the changed design. The open question is how much independent checking of an automatically derived dependency slice is enough to justify reusing the remaining evidence, without incurring the full cost of reconstructing that evidence on every revision.

## Summary

The transfer test turns source-to-target differences into a plan for requalification or a new architectural study. An admission check asks whether the decision itself survived the move; four stages then assign each unit an action and pair changed dependencies with checks able to observe the resulting risk. In the prospective Lighthouse application (@sec-intent-vs-spec), simulator outputs and candidate identities remain useful historical material. Workload coverage, the executable software path, memory costs, and implementation behavior still need target evidence. Exploration can reuse source work while leaving room to generate and evaluate different hardware and software organizations when the target requires them.

Transfer must also survive the software path. A transferred offload or kernel result carries a compiler version inside it, and a comparison that pins the hardware but not the toolchain can mistake compiler maturity for a hardware gain.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Components move, conclusions do not.** Data sources, models, tool paths, and checks remain reusable while their invariants and dependencies hold; a source conclusion remains applicable only where its supporting conditions still hold. Changed or uncertain dependencies require new evidence.
- **The transfer test.** Check whether the decision has changed, then partition the source, isolate the affected slice, assign each unit an action, and enforce target checks.
- **Materiality is claim-specific.** A change reopens a claim when it alters the candidate identity, executable path, measured quantity, objective, decision rule, ranking, constraint verdict, or physical mechanism; magnitude alone decides nothing.
- **Transfer benefit needs a matched arm.** A carried prior earns its place only against a target-only arm with the same tasks, budgets, and stopping rules, with adaptation and requalification charged to the transfer.
- **Version-paired evaluation.** Retain hardware and software snapshots with the inputs and procedures needed to repeat a comparison, then test software sensitivity before attributing a gain to microarchitecture alone.
:::

The next step is to evaluate the complete approach across repeated, varied, and adversarial architectural studies (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). The source-to-target map identifies which claims each changed study must establish. Those comparisons can then test whether an AI-native design system improves the architecture result, reduces the total engineering cost of achieving it, or does both.
